claim: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a liver tumor that usually arises in patients with cirrhosis.
source: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a liver tumor that usually arises in patients with cirrhosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction (Calderaro et al., 2019).

claim: Hepatic stellate cells are key players in the progression of HCC.
source: Hepatic stellate cells are key players in the progression of HCC, as they create a fibrotic micro-environment and produce growth factors and cytokines that enhance tumor cell proliferation and migration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: Hepatic stellate cells create a fibrotic micro-environment that enhances tumor cell proliferation and migration.
source: Hepatic stellate cells are key players in the progression of HCC, as they create a fibrotic micro-environment and produce growth factors and cytokines that enhance tumor cell proliferation and migration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Treatment with the IRE1α-inhibitor 4μ8C reduced tumor burden in mice with fibrotic HCC.
source: Mice with a fibrotic HCC were treated with the IRE1α-inhibitor 4μ8C, which reduced tumor burden and collagen deposition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Treatment with 4μ8C reduced collagen deposition in mice with fibrotic HCC.
source: Mice with a fibrotic HCC were treated with the IRE1α-inhibitor 4μ8C, which reduced tumor burden and collagen deposition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HCC-cells activate IRE1α in stellate cells, thereby contributing to their activation.
source: By co-culturing HCC-cells with stellate cells, we found that HCC-cells activate IREα in stellate cells, thereby contributing to their activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by co-culture experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Inhibiting IRE1α blocked stellate cell activation.
source: Inhibiting IRE1α blocked stellate cell activation, which then decreased proliferation and migration of tumor cells in different in vitro 2D and 3D co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4, 6, and 8.

claim: Blocking stellate cell activation decreased proliferation of tumor cells in co-cultures.
source: Inhibiting IRE1α blocked stellate cell activation, which then decreased proliferation and migration of tumor cells in different in vitro 2D and 3D co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Blocking stellate cell activation decreased migration of tumor cells in co-cultures.
source: Inhibiting IRE1α blocked stellate cell activation, which then decreased proliferation and migration of tumor cells in different in vitro 2D and 3D co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: There are cell-line-specific direct effects of inhibiting IRE1α in tumor cells.
source: In addition, we also observed cell-line-specific direct effects of inhibiting IRE1α in tumor cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 9.

claim: Hepatocellular carcinoma typically arises in a background of chronic liver disease and cirrhosis.
source: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a primary liver tumor that typically arises in a background of chronic liver disease and cirrhosis (Calderaro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Hepatic stellate cells differentiate towards contractile myofibroblast-like cells that deposit extracellular matrix proteins during liver damage.
source: One of the key players in the progression of cirrhosis to HCC is the hepatic stellate cell, which is activated during liver damage and differentiates towards a contractile myofibroblast-like cell that deposits extracellular matrix proteins (ECM), such as collagen (Coulouarn and Clément, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Activated stellate cells induce phenotypic changes in cancer cells through the production of growth factors and cytokines.
source: Activated stellate cells can induce phenotypic changes in cancer cells through the production of growth factors and cytokines that stimulate tumor cell proliferation and induce a pro-metastatic phenotype (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Malignant hepatocytes secrete high levels of transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ).
source: Malignant hepatocytes secrete high levels of transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ), which can contribute to the activation of stellate cells in the nearby stroma (Giannelli et al., 2014; Nitta et al., 2008; Dooley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: TGFβ secreted by malignant hepatocytes contributes to the activation of stellate cells in the nearby stroma.
source: Malignant hepatocytes secrete high levels of transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ), which can contribute to the activation of stellate cells in the nearby stroma (Giannelli et al., 2014; Nitta et al., 2008; Dooley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: ECM-components such as proteoglycans, collagens, laminin, and fibronectin interact with tumor cells and can directly promote cellular transformation and metastasis.
source: Several of the ECM-components such as proteoglycans, collagens, laminin, and fibronectin interact with tumor cells and cells in the stroma, which can directly promote cellular transformation and metastasis (Lin et al., 2014; Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The ECM can act as a reservoir for growth factors and cytokines.
source: The ECM can also act as a reservoir for growth factors and cytokines, which can be rapidly released to support the tumor's needs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge.

claim: Activated stellate cells contribute to a highly vascularized tumor micro-environment by secreting pro-angiogenic molecules.
source: In addition, activated stellate cells contribute to a highly vascularized tumor micro-environment, by secreting pro-angiogenic molecules and by recruiting pro-angiogenic (and pro-tumoral) myeloid and lymphoid derived cell types (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Activated stellate cells cause hypoxia by constricting the hepatic microvasculature.
source: By constricting the hepatic microvasculature, they also cause hypoxia, which contributes to the angiogenic switch and can induce a more aggressive tumor phenotype (Taura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Hypoxia contributes to the angiogenic switch and can induce a more aggressive tumor phenotype.
source: By constricting the hepatic microvasculature, they also cause hypoxia, which contributes to the angiogenic switch and can induce a more aggressive tumor phenotype (Taura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Tumor cells actively secrete growth factors such as TGFβ to induce activation and migration of stellate cells.
source: It is therefore not surprising that tumor cells actively secrete growth factors (such as TGFβ) to induce activation and migration of stellate cells, which creates a fibrotic environment that further supports and enhances tumor progression (Coulouarn and Clément, 2014; Caja et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Blocking stellate cell activation has been proposed as a potential therapy for patients with HCC.
source: Since activated stellate cells play an essential role in the onset and progression of HCC, blocking their activation has been proposed as a potential therapy for patients with HCC (Carloni et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Blocking the IRE1α-pathway of the unfolded protein response is one strategy to prevent stellate cell activation.
source: One strategy to prevent stellate cell activation, is by blocking the IRE1α-pathway of the unfolded protein response (UPR) (Heindryckx et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The UPR serves to cope with the accumulation of misfolded or unfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: The UPR serves to cope with the accumulation of misfolded or unfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in an attempt to restore protein folding, increase ER-biosynthetic machinery and maintain cellular homeostasis (Schröder and Kaufman, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The UPR can exert a cytoprotective effect by re-establishing cellular homeostasis.
source: It can exert a cytoprotective effect by re-establishing cellular homeostasis, while apoptotic signaling pathways will be activated in case of severe and/or prolonged ER-stress (Lam et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Apoptotic signaling pathways are activated in case of severe and/or prolonged ER-stress.
source: It can exert a cytoprotective effect by re-establishing cellular homeostasis, while apoptotic signaling pathways will be activated in case of severe and/or prolonged ER-stress (Lam et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The presence of misfolded proteins is sensed via three transmembrane proteins in the ER: IRE1α, PERK and ATF6α.
source: The presence of misfolded proteins is sensed via three transmembrane proteins in the ER: inositol requiring enzyme 1α (IRE1α), protein kinase RNA-like ER-kinase (PERK) and activating transcription factor 6α (ATF6α) (Acosta-Alvear et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The development of solid tumors is characterized by uncontrolled growth and proliferation of malignant cells, resulting in a compact mass of cells and a hypoxic tumor micro-environment.
source: The development of solid tumors is characterized by uncontrolled growth and proliferation of malignant cells, resulting in a compact mass of cells and a hypoxic tumor micro-environment, two conditions that are well-characterized ER-stress inducers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge.

claim: A compact mass of cells and a hypoxic tumor micro-environment are well-characterized ER-stress inducers.
source: The development of solid tumors is characterized by uncontrolled growth and proliferation of malignant cells, resulting in a compact mass of cells and a hypoxic tumor micro-environment, two conditions that are well-characterized ER-stress inducers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge.

claim: Activation of the UPR represents a major hallmark of several solid tumors, such as breast cancer, colon cancer, and HCC.
source: Therefore, it is not surprising that activation of the UPR represents a major hallmark of several solid tumors, such as breast cancer (Liang et al., 2018), colon cancer (Li et al., 2017b), and HCC (Vandewynckel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The induction of the UPR in cancer cells may serve as a double-edged sword, which can aid tumor progression as well as prevent tumor growth in a context-dependent manner.
source: The induction of the UPR in cancer cells may serve as a double-edged sword, which can aid tumor progression as well as prevent tumor growth in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents an interpretation of the literature.

claim: Persistent ER-stress can activate pathways that induce cell death, effectively eliminating cells with a potential to become malignant.
source: Persistent ER-stress can activate pathways that induce cell death, effectively eliminating cells with a potential to become malignant.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge.

claim: Tumor cells may hijack the ER-stress pathways to provide survival signals required for uncontrolled growth and eventually avoid apoptosis.
source: On the other hand, tumor cells may hijack the ER-stress pathways to provide survival signals required for uncontrolled growth and eventually avoid apoptosis (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Activation of the UPR has been shown to affect different fibrotic diseases.
source: Activation of the UPR has also been shown to affect different fibrotic diseases (Heindryckx and Li, 2018), including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (Bandla et al., 2018; Kwanten et al., 2016; Dasgupta et al., 2020), hepatitis-B-induced carcinogenesis (Li et al., 2017a), and biliary cirrhosis (Sasaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Inhibiting the IRE1α-branch of the UPR-pathway using 4μ8C blocks TGFβ-induced activation of fibroblasts and stellate cells in vitro.
source: We have previously shown that inhibiting the IRE1α-branch of the UPR-pathway using 4μ8C, blocks TGFβ-induced activation of fibroblasts and stellate cells in vitro and reduces liver fibrosis in vivo (Heindryckx et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Inhibiting the IRE1α-branch of the UPR-pathway using 4μ8C reduces liver fibrosis in vivo.
source: We have previously shown that inhibiting the IRE1α-branch of the UPR-pathway using 4μ8C, blocks TGFβ-induced activation of fibroblasts and stellate cells in vitro and reduces liver fibrosis in vivo (Heindryckx et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of the IRE1α-signaling pathway decreases tumor burden in a chemically induced mouse model for HCC.
source: We show that pharmacologic inhibition of the IRE1α-signaling pathway decreases tumor burden in a chemically induced mouse model for HCC.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 1B.

claim: Blocking IRE1α in hepatic stellate cells prevents their activation.
source: Using several in vitro co-culturing methods, we identified that blocking IRE1α in hepatic stellate cells prevents their activation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 9.

claim: There are cell-line-specific differences in how cells respond to IRE1α-inhibition.
source: Our results also indicate that there are cell-line-specific differences in how cells respond to IRE1α-inhibition, including differences in the IRE1α-dependent generation of reactive oxygen species.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: There are differences in the IRE1α-dependent generation of reactive oxygen species between cell lines.
source: Our results also indicate that there are cell-line-specific differences in how cells respond to IRE1α-inhibition, including differences in the IRE1α-dependent generation of reactive oxygen species.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 10.

claim: Histological analysis of liver tissue confirmed the presence of liver tumors in a fibrotic background at 25 weeks in DEN-treated mice.
source: Histological analysis of liver tissue confirmed the presence of liver tumors in a fibrotic background at 25 weeks (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by histological images in Figure 1A.

claim: Treatment with 4μ8C significantly reduced tumor burden in DEN-induced mice.
source: Treatment with 4μ8C significantly reduced tumor burden (Figure 1B), as measured on H and E-stained liver sections (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1B.

claim: Mice with HCC had a significant increase in the percentage of collagen compared to healthy mice.
source: Mice with HCC had a significant increase in the percentage of collagen (Figure 1C) and αSMA-staining (Figure 1D), compared to healthy mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1C.

claim: Mice with HCC had a significant increase in αSMA-staining compared to healthy mice.
source: Mice with HCC had a significant increase in the percentage of collagen (Figure 1C) and αSMA-staining (Figure 1D), compared to healthy mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: Treatment with 4μ8C restored collagen levels to healthy baseline levels.
source: Treatment with 4μ8C restored collagen (Figure 1C) and αSMA-levels (Figure 1D and Figure 1E) to healthy baseline levels.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment with 4μ8C restored αSMA-levels to healthy baseline levels.
source: Treatment with 4μ8C restored collagen (Figure 1C) and αSMA-levels (Figure 1D and Figure 1E) to healthy baseline levels.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: Proliferation of cells was increased within the tumor itself, compared to the levels in healthy liver tissue and stromal tissue.
source: As expected, proliferation of cells was increased within the tumor itself, compared to the levels in healthy liver tissue and stromal tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PCNA mRNA expression data in Figure 1E.

claim: Treatment with 4μ8C significantly decreased the levels of Pcna-mRNA expression within the tumor.
source: Treatment with 4μ8C significantly decreased the levels of Pcna-mRNA expression within the tumor, suggesting a decrease in tumor cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: DEN-induced murine tumors had a significantly increased protein expression of 20 oncogenic proteins compared to healthy controls.
source: A proteomics array using the Olink Mouse Exploratory assay revealed that DEN-induced murine tumors had a significantly increased protein expression of 20 oncogenic proteins compared to healthy controls (Figure 1F and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proteomics data in Figure 1F and Table 1.

claim: In the 4μ8C-treated group, only 11 oncogenic proteins were increased compared to healthy controls.
source: In the 4μ8C-treated group, only 11 oncogenic proteins were increased compared to healthy controls (Figure 1F and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proteomics data in Figure 1F and Table 1.

claim: Treatment with 4μ8C significantly reduced protein expression of PRDX5 and DDAH1.
source: Treatment with 4μ8C also significantly reduced protein expression of two HCC promotors, PRDX5, and DDAH1 (Figure 1F and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proteomics data in Figure 1F and Table 1.

claim: Hspa5-mRNA-expression was increased in the surrounding non-tumor tissue of DEN-induced mice with HCC.
source: Hspa5-mRNA-expression was increased in the surrounding non-tumor tissue of DEN-induced mice with HCC, while there was no difference within the tumor, compared to healthy controls (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: There was no difference in Hspa5-mRNA-expression within the tumor, compared to healthy controls.
source: Hspa5-mRNA-expression was increased in the surrounding non-tumor tissue of DEN-induced mice with HCC, while there was no difference within the tumor, compared to healthy controls (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Western blot confirmed the increase of BIP-protein expression in DEN-induced livers.
source: Western blot confirmed the increase of BIP-protein expression in DEN-induced livers, which was reduced after treatment with 4μ8C (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: BIP-protein expression was reduced after treatment with 4μ8C.
source: Western blot confirmed the increase of BIP-protein expression in DEN-induced livers, which was reduced after treatment with 4μ8C (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: The ratio of spliced to unspliced Xbp1-mRNA was significantly increased in the surrounding non-tumor tissue of DEN-induced mice.
source: The ratio of spliced to unspliced Xbp1-mRNA was significantly increased in the surrounding non-tumor tissue of DEN-induced mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment with 4μ8C significantly reduced the ratio of spliced to unspliced Xbp1-mRNA in surrounding non-tumorous stromal tissue.
source: Treatment with 4μ8C significantly reduced the ratio of spliced to unspliced Xbp1-mRNA in surrounding non-tumorous stromal tissue (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Western blot confirmed a significant decrease of XBP1-splicing after treatment with 4μ8C.
source: Western blot on whole tissue samples – containing both tumor and non-tumoral tissue – also confirmed a significant decrease of XBP1-splicing after treatment with 4μ8C (Figure 2E,F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 2E, F, and G.

claim: The expression of spliced XBP1 is mainly located in the peritumoral area.
source: Immunohistochemical straining with XBP1-antibodies against the spliced variant further demonstrate that the expression of spliced XBP1 is mainly located in the peritumoral area (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunohistochemical images in Figure 2H.

claim: Spliced XBP1 was significantly increased in the DEN-induced liver tissue.
source: Spliced XBP1 was significantly increased in the DEN-induced liver tissue and treatment with 4μ8C restored these levels to a similar level as seen in healthy controls (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 2I.

claim: Treatment with 4μ8C restored spliced XBP1 levels to a similar level as seen in healthy controls.
source: Spliced XBP1 was significantly increased in the DEN-induced liver tissue and treatment with 4μ8C restored these levels to a similar level as seen in healthy controls (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 2I.

claim: Expression of markers from the IRE1α-pathway were mainly localized within activated stellate cells in the liver.
source: Co-staining of liver tissue with antibodies against αSMA and antibodies against spliced XBP1 (Figure 2—figure supplements 1A and 2A), total XBP1 (Figure 2—figure supplements 1B and 2B), IRE1α (Figure 2—figure supplements 1C and 2C), phospho-IRE1α (Figure 2—figure supplements 1D and 2D), and BIP (Figure 2—figure supplements 1E and 2E), revealed that expression of markers from the IRE1α-pathway were mainly localized within activated stellate cells in the liver, although other hepatic cell populations also expressed some of these markers.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-staining images in Figure 2 supplements.

claim: Other hepatic cell populations also expressed some IRE1α-pathway markers.
source: Co-staining of liver tissue with antibodies against αSMA and antibodies against spliced XBP1 (Figure 2—figure supplements 1A and 2A), total XBP1 (Figure 2—figure supplements 1B and 2B), IRE1α (Figure 2—figure supplements 1C and 2C), phospho-IRE1α (Figure 2—figure supplements 1D and 2D), and BIP (Figure 2—figure supplements 1E and 2E), revealed that expression of markers from the IRE1α-pathway were mainly localized within activated stellate cells in the liver, although other hepatic cell populations also expressed some of these markers.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-staining images in Figure 2 supplements.

claim: The expression of spliced XBP1 is not only cytoplasmic but some staining appears peri-nuclear and nuclear.
source: At a higher magnification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), it also becomes clear that the expression of spliced XBP1 is not only cytoplasmic but some staining appears peri-nuclear and nuclear.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by high magnification images in Figure 2 supplement 1F.

claim: A gene-set enrichment assay on microarray data from HCC-patients showed an increase of genes involved in the UPR in the fibrotic HCC samples compared to non-fibrous HCC.
source: A gene-set enrichment assay on microarray data from HCC-patients with fibrotic septae and without fibrotic septae showed an increase of genes involved in the UPR in the fibrotic HCC samples compared to non-fibrous HCC (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by GSEA data in Figure 3A.

claim: Several actors of the IRE1α-branch of the UPR are amongst the genes that contribute to the core-enrichment of the GSEA analysis.
source: Several actors of the IRE1α-branch of the UPR are amongst the genes that contribute to the core-enrichment of this analysis (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining of liver biopsies from HCC-patients confirmed presence of IRE1α-mediated ER-stress markers BIP, PPP2R5B, SHC1, and WIPI1 localized in the fibrotic scar tissue and near hepatic blood vessels.
source: Immunohistochemical staining of liver biopsies from HCC-patients further confirmed presence of IRE1α-mediated ER-stress markers BIP, PPP2R5B, SHC1, and WIPI1 localized in the fibrotic scar tissue and near hepatic blood vessels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunohistochemical images in Figure 3B.

claim: Increased expression of BIP, PPP2R5B, SHC1, and WIPI1 was significantly correlated with poor survival in patients with liver cancer.
source: In addition, increased expression of these markers was significantly correlated with poor survival in patients with liver cancer (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curves in Figure 3C.

claim: Tumor cells secrete factors that induce mRNA-expression of EIF2AK3, DDIT3, and HSPA5 in hepatic stellate cells.
source: This confirmed that tumor cells secrete factors that induce mRNA-expression of EIF2AK3, DDIT3, HSPA5 (Figure 4A), spliced XBP1 (Figure 4B,C and D), and HSPA5 (Figure 4C), as well as protein expression of p-IRE1α (Figure 4F) in hepatic stellate cells co-cultured with tumor cells, indicating the presence of ER-stress.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-culture data in Figure 4A.

claim: Tumor cells secrete factors that induce spliced XBP1 in hepatic stellate cells.
source: This confirmed that tumor cells secrete factors that induce mRNA-expression of EIF2AK3, DDIT3, HSPA5 (Figure 4A), spliced XBP1 (Figure 4B,C and D), and HSPA5 (Figure 4C), as well as protein expression of p-IRE1α (Figure 4F) in hepatic stellate cells co-cultured with tumor cells, indicating the presence of ER-stress.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-culture data in Figure 4B, C, and D.

claim: Tumor cells secrete factors that induce protein expression of p-IRE1α in hepatic stellate cells.
source: This confirmed that tumor cells secrete factors that induce mRNA-expression of EIF2AK3, DDIT3, HSPA5 (Figure 4A), spliced XBP1 (Figure 4B,C and D), and HSPA5 (Figure 4C), as well as protein expression of p-IRE1α (Figure 4F) in hepatic stellate cells co-cultured with tumor cells, indicating the presence of ER-stress.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 4F.

claim: Co-culturing tumor cells with stellate cells led to stellate cell activation, as measured by mRNA-expression of ACTA2 and collagen.
source: Co-culturing also led to their activation, as measured by mRNA-expression of ACTA2 (Figure 4F) and collagen (Figure 4G) in LX2-cells grown with HepG2 or Huh7-cells in a transwell-assay.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-culture data in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Adding 4μ8C to transwell co-cultures restored the mRNA-expression of ACTA2 and collagen to baseline levels.
source: The mRNA-expression of ACTA2 and collagen was restored to baseline levels when 4μ8C was added to the transwell co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-culture data in Figure 4F and G.

claim: LX2-cells and HepG2-cells successfully engrafted the collagen-rich matrix of the decellularized human liver scaffolds.
source: Sirius red staining and H and E staining confirmed that that LX2-cells and HepG2-cells successfully engrafted the collagen-rich matrix of the decellularized human liver scaffolds (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by histological images in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Engrafting both LX2-stellate cells and HepG2-cancer cells led to a significant increase of collagen staining compared to scaffolds that were only engrafted with LX2-cells.
source: Engrafting both LX2-stellate cells and HepG2-cancer cells led to a significant increase of collagen staining (Figure 5B) and mRNA-expression of collagen, HSPA5, and spliced XBP1 (Figure 5C) compared to scaffolds that were only engrafted with LX2-cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: Engrafting both LX2-stellate cells and HepG2-cancer cells led to a significant increase of mRNA-expression of collagen, HSPA5, and spliced XBP1 compared to scaffolds that were only engrafted with LX2-cells.
source: Engrafting both LX2-stellate cells and HepG2-cancer cells led to a significant increase of collagen staining (Figure 5B) and mRNA-expression of collagen, HSPA5, and spliced XBP1 (Figure 5C) compared to scaffolds that were only engrafted with LX2-cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Adding 4μ8C significantly decreased mRNA-expression of collagen and HSPA5 in the LX2 and HepG2 co-cultured scaffolds.
source: Adding 4μ8C significantly decreased mRNA-expression of collagen and HSPA5 in the LX2 and HepG2 co-cultured scaffolds (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Measuring TGFβ in mono-cultures lead to undetectable levels of TGFβ in Huh7-cells and low-levels in HepG2-cells.
source: Surprisingly, measuring TGFβ in mono-cultures lead to undetectable levels of TGFβ in Huh7-cells and low-levels in HepG2-cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 4 supplement 1A.

claim: TGFβ levels increased when LX2-cells were added to the co-cultures.
source: These levels increased when LX2-cells were added to the co-cultures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 4 supplement 1A.

claim: Engrafting both LX2-stellate cells and HepG2-cancer cells in the human liver scaffolds slightly increased TGFβ-levels in the medium compared to scaffolds engrafted by only one cell type, but overall no significant differences were seen.
source: Engrafting both LX2-stellate cells and HepG2-cancer cells in the human liver scaffolds, slightly increased TGFβ-levels in the medium compared to scaffolds engrafted by only one cell type, but overall no significant differences were seen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data in Figure 4 supplement 1B.

claim: The baseline TGFβ-levels were markedly higher in the mono-cultured scaffolds, compared to the levels measured in cells grown in a standard 2D in vitro set-up.
source: It is important to note that the baseline TGFβ-levels were markedly higher in the mono-cultured scaffolds, compared to the levels measured in cells grown in a standard 2D in vitro set-up (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by comparison of ELISA data in Figure 4 supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Blocking TGFβ-receptor signaling with SB-431541 significantly reduced mRNA-expression of ER-stress markers DDIT3, spliced XBP1 and HSPA5 in stellate cells co-cultured with tumor cells.
source: Blocking TGFβ-receptor signaling with SB-431541 significantly reduced mRNA-expression of ER-stress markers DDIT3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), spliced XBP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and HSPA5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) in stellate cells co-cultured with tumor cells using transwells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4 supplement 1C, D, and F.

claim: Adding a TGFβ-receptor-inhibitor to stellate cell – tumor cell co-cultures reduced stellate cell activation, as measured by mRNA-expression of ACTA2 and collagen.
source: Adding a TGFβ-receptor-inhibitor to stellate cell – tumor cell co-cultures also reduced stellate cell activation, as measured by mRNA-expression of ACTA2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G) and collagen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4 supplement 1G and H.

claim: TGFβ-secretion by tumor cells could be, at least in part, responsible for activating stellate cells and for inducing the IRE1α-branch of the UPR.
source: This indicates that TGFβ-secretion by tumor cells could be, at least in part, responsible for activating stellate cells and for inducing the IRE1α-branch of the UPR.
